stops.name: Stuttgart, the first Waldorf School opens on the Uhlandshöhe
stops.campa: On 7 September 1919 the Free Waldorf School opens with festival and song: two hundred fifty-six children in eight grades, the greater number of them from the families of the factory floor. Steiner speaks of the school as a deed of culture, a renewal of the spiritual life of the age from the child upward; Molt has given the building on the Uhlandshöhe; the teachers stand consecrated by the August course. The stationmaster's son who walked across a border to his schooling has founded the school without borders. Within his lifetime it will be the largest free school in Germany, and after it, a world movement.

stops.name: Dornach, the first Goetheanum opens its courses
stops.campa: On 26 September 1920 the building opens, unfinished, as sacred buildings are, with the first course of the School of Spiritual Science: three weeks, thirty lecturers, doctors and physicists and jurists testing their sciences against the science of the spirit. The two unequal domes interpenetrate above the hill like two thoughts becoming one; the carved columns progress through their planetary metamorphoses; the glass windows glow with engraved visions. The house is called Goetheanum, for the man who first saw metamorphosis. In the white hall under the domes, the word that began in a station waiting room has built itself a body.

stops.name: Arlesheim, the clinic of Ita Wegman
stops.campa: In the neighboring village of Arlesheim the Dutch physician Ita Wegman opens the Clinical-Therapeutic Institute, and the medicine of the movement receives its house. Steiner has given the doctors their courses; now, with Wegman, the healing work becomes daily practice: mistletoe against the crab-disease, the remedies of metal and plant, the physician's diagnosis extended by the seer's reading of karma. Between Wegman and Steiner grows the deepest working friendship of the late years; with her he will write his last book, and to her care he will entrust his own final illness.

stops.name: Munich, the tumult at the Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten
stops.campa: On a lecture tour through the great halls of Germany, twelve cities, thousands nightly, the hatred of the new nationalism finds him. In the Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten at Munich on 15 May 1922, as he ends his lecture, a band of völkisch youths storms toward the platform; the lights are cut; friends close around him and bring him out through a side door as the brawl breaks behind them. The canon marks the sign coldly: in the Germany that is coming, the teacher of freedom can no longer speak in public halls. He does not lecture publicly in Germany again.

stops.name: Vienna, the East-West Congress
stops.campa: In June 1922 he returns in triumph to the city of his studenthood: the East-West Congress in the Vienna Musikverein, ten evenings before two thousand hearers, the greatest outer success of his life. He speaks of the cosmic thoughts of the East and the natural science of the West, and of anthroposophy as the bridge on which they may meet without either abasing itself. The student who once rode in from Inzersdorf with Felix's herbs in the luggage rack above him now fills the golden hall. Vienna listens, applauds, and the hour of public triumphs is already closing.

stops.name: Oxford, Spiritual Values in Education
stops.campa: At Manchester College, Oxford, in August 1922, he gives the course Spiritual Values in Education and Social Life to the schoolmasters of England, and the English press writes with astonishment of the Austrian doctor's Grün ideas arriving with Viennese courtesy and mathematical calm. From Oxford the Waldorf impulse crosses into the English tongue; schools will follow in Britain within the decade. The lecture journeys now ring the continent's edge: Stratford, Oxford, Torquay, Penmaenmawr, as if the word, pressed out of Germany's halls, were seeking the islands.

stops.name: Dornach, New Year's Eve: the Goetheanum burns
stops.campa: On the last evening of 1922 the members hear a eurythmy performance, then their teacher's lecture in the great hall; the ten years' work of seventeen nations stands complete around them. In the night, smoke is found in the white hall: fire, set in the wall's hollow by an unknown hand, runs hidden between the domes. All night the building burns; the fire brigades of the villages and the members in a human chain cannot hold it; toward morning the two domes fall in upon the organ and the glass. Steiner stands on the hill through it all, silent, watching the work of his life go up in flame.

stops.name: Dornach, the Schreinerei, next morning: the work continues
stops.campa: On the morning of New Year's Day the ruin still smokes on the hill. Steiner orders the flooded, soot-blackened joinery shed, the Schreinerei, where the building was born, cleaned by evening, and announces that the program proceeds as printed. That night, meters from the embers, he continues the course on the origins of natural science at the appointed hour, without a word of lamentation in the lecture itself. The canon fixes the scene at the center of the whole biography: the building can burn; the work cannot. Grief is given no authority over the task.
stops.quote: We will go on with our lectures as notified.
stops.quote_source: As recorded by Albert Steffen, Dornach, 1 January 1923

stops.name: Dornach, the pledge to the workers
stops.campa: To the workmen of the Goetheanum, gathered in the days after the fire, he gives his word plainly, in the workman's own register: nothing that has happened, and nothing that may yet happen, will turn him from his path. The insurance assessors move through the ashes; the enemies in the press exult; within the Society the year of crisis begins. He lectures on through it all: on the year's course as breathing of the earth, on the history of the movement, unsparing toward his own members. The ruin on the hill becomes the sternest of his teachers, and he uses it.
stops.quote: As long as I live, I will represent my cause and represent it in the same way as I have represented it up to now.
stops.quote_source: Address to the workers at the Goetheanum, 5 January 1923

stops.name: Penmaenmawr, the mysteries of the Druids
stops.campa: In August 1923 he travels into Wales, to Penmaenmawr above the sea, where the stone circles of the Druids stand on the mountain shoulder. He climbs to the circles and reads them as an initiate reads a ruined script: here the priests of the old sun-mystery observed the shadow-tones of the light, and the spiritual world, he says, stands nearer in this air than almost anywhere in Europe. The lectures given there on the evolution of consciousness he will count among his most penetrating. On the burnt foundation of the new mysteries, he grafts the memory of the oldest ones of the West.

stops.name: Dornach, the Christmas Conference opens
stops.campa: At Christmas 1923 some eight hundred members from all countries crowd the Schreinerei beside the ruin. Steiner, who has stood apart from every office, announces the unheard-of: he will himself take the presidency of a newly founded General Anthroposophical Society, binding his personal destiny and his esoteric task to the earthly institution, a deed, he says, of highest risk before the spiritual world. The society is to be utterly open and utterly esoteric at once; its constitution is laid down in principles read aloud like a ritual text. The refounding begins on Christmas Eve, in a wooden shed, beside ashes.

stops.name: Dornach, the Foundation Stone laid in the hearts
stops.campa: On Christmas morning he lays the new foundation stone, and this time no copper form in the earth: it is a meditation, the Foundation Stone of love, formed out of the universal word, lowered into the hearts of the members as its only ground. Soul of Man! The verses sound for the first time, speaking to limbs, heart and head, to the depths, the circumference and the heights; through the conference's seven days he turns the stone rhythm by rhythm like a jewel. What was burnt as a building is refounded as a community of hearts. The esoteric history of the movement calls this its central deed.
stops.quote: Let us here and now lay in the ground of our hearts the dodecahedral Foundation Stone of love.
stops.quote_source: Address at the laying of the Foundation Stone, Christmas Conference, Dornach, 25 December 1923
